extracted.intended_audience: Carpentries instructor trainees and workshop instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructors preparing to teach Carpentries workshops, focusing on learner-centered planning, formative assessment, learning objectives, and team coordination rather than technical deep-dives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching is a skill; requires deliberate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching is a skill - and a complex one at that. Whether you are new to teaching or skilled in certain methods, adding new features takes time, effort, and deliberate practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate time and deliberate practice to develop new teaching methods. Recognize that practice without feedback can solidify bad habits; seek feedback and alter behavior in response. Use this episode as an ongoing reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise learner-centered preparation over technical over-preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over-prepare on technical content – which can be endless! – and under-prepare the learner-centered elements of your teaching practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set aside time before deeply reviewing technical content to plan your approach to instruction. If you encounter questions you can’t answer, demonstrating how you Google things can be beneficial. Focus first on audience and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: To teach effectively, you have to know who you are teaching. Consider learners in a broader context and reserve time to think through how their experiences and needs may differ from your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine a learner: their background, problems, and gains from the workshop. Recognize limits (you won't know everything about individuals, neurodiversity, personal circumstances) and plan inclusively to support varied needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pre-workshop surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember Your Pre-Workshop Surveys: The Carpentries strives to create useful assessment instruments that can help you plan and understand your workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the links sent by The Carpentries Workshops and Instruction Team for up-to-date participant data; use survey results (which may accumulate up to start time) to tailor instruction. Suggest improvements to surveys when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine learning objectives (lessons list objectives at top)
rubrics_metrics.description: All Carpentries lessons should have learning objectives listed at the top of each episode. In most cases they are quite specific about what a learner should be able to do by the end of the episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objectives to design formative assessments and to evaluate potential additions or digressions for appropriateness. Locate objectives at episode start and let them guide pacing and content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objectives should target novice learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Carpentries learning objectives should target novice learners. This typically means that the actions specified by the learning objective should be basic and uncomplicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbs like 'recognise,' 'distinguish,' or 'use.' Avoid verbs such as 'design,' 'evaluate,' or 'break down' that imply higher cognitive complexity when the target is a novice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make objectives specific and assessable; avoid vague verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'know' and 'understand' are difficult to use when assessing whether a learner has met an objective; they are ambiguous with regard to level of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve such objectives by making them specific to an outcome that is clearly achievable and readily assessed. Replace vague verbs with observable, testable actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the urge to complicate / expert awareness gap
rubrics_metrics.description: When experts teach, they are often eager to advance learners to higher cognitive levels, which can skip steps and cause cognitive overload (expert awareness gap).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking for higher-order tasks (synthesis, creation) before fundamentals are secured. Identify underlying knowledge required at each step; consult Bloom's Taxonomy to choose appropriate cognitive levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare to use formative assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a learning objective has been met, everyone should know about it. Formative assessment supports metacognition and motivates learners by making achievement visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build checkpoints where learners can demonstrate achievement. Use multiple formats (MCQs, exercises, spontaneous questions, sticky notes) to verify mastery and inform both instructor and learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify checkpoints in a lesson for formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify where in the episode a learning objective should reasonably be achieved and consider how formative assessment might be used most effectively at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map objectives to specific moments in the lesson, then choose targeted assessments to both verify achievement and explicitly inform learners of their progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment frequency: every 5–15 minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should use a formative assessment ideally every 5 minutes and at least every 10-15 minutes to make sure the class is actually learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent assessments help maintain attention, break up instruction, and allow skipping already-known material. Use quick checks often rather than infrequent broad checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Do you understand?" is ineffective as formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners are often reluctant to admit when they do not understand; self-assessments without targeted checks are inaccurate because of the Dunning-Kruger effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking the room 'Do you understand?'. Instead, use targeted formative assessment to remove reliance on self-judgement and to generate reliable information about learners' levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare to cut content thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative maintenance leads to curricula that can be long; you will likely need to make cuts to what you plan to teach to stay on schedule and allow for formative assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan cuts in advance to avoid mistakes when cutting on the fly. Consider knock-on effects and prioritize learning objectives over simply covering material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep breaks on time
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep breaks on time even if your content is split awkwardly around them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying breaks can demotivate learners and disrupt their plans; maintain scheduled break times even when pacing is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for dependencies when cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch out for dependencies if you skip a step; it may generate or re-name a file that is used in later episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before cutting, check for downstream dependencies and communicate with team/learners about skipped steps and how to access missing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave time to wrap up the workshop
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave time to wrap up your workshop even if this means cutting even more content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize closure; a good wrap-up helps learners synthesize and know next steps. Allocate explicit wrap-up time when planning cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not speed up to cover missed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not speed up if you are running behind; quickly covering (but not actually teaching) content has little value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that curricula are freely available and learners can revisit missed content; it's better to omit than to rush through without learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate with your team about cuts and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate with your team about what you plan to cut, or what you decided to leave out. Do not assume anyone will notice if you skip something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team members may help fit missed concepts into later content if they know what's been skipped; share plans and coordinate adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate with learners about skipped content and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate with your learners about where they can find skipped content and whether any help may be available to support their independent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain omissions to reduce anxiety and give clear directions for follow-up resources and support options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the instructor notes and community troubleshooting pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Many lessons have instructor's notes linked under 'Extras' and community-developed pages document configuration problems and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult instructor notes when teaching a lesson for the first time. Use documented solutions for common technical hurdles and contribute new problems/solutions back to the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review prior feedback and use reflective practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Review post-workshop survey responses and other feedback after a workshop and again before your next workshop to refresh memories of successes and challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief reflective practice to decide what to keep and what to change. Emphasize feedback-informed changes over mere repetition to avoid solidifying bad habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with and prepare alongside your teaching team
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative feedback review with team-members you have taught with previously is valuable; some independent preparation steps can be done collaboratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare with your team to create a cohesive classroom experience and to share insights from prior teaching. Use collaborative rehearsal or feedback sessions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minute cards / sticky notes to collect ongoing feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Use your sticky notes or the form provided by your Trainers to write minute cards as discussed in part 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect quick, in-class signals about learner status and revisit them to inform pacing and remediation during the workshop.
